subject: Chemistry
title: Atomic Structure
learningOutcomes: Explain the structure of the atom as a central nucleus containing neutrons and protons, surrounded by electrons in shells.
State that orbits (shells) are energy levels of electrons, and a larger shell implies higher energy and greater average distance from the nucleus.
State that electrons are quantum particles with probabilistic paths whose exact paths and locations cannot be mapped (with reference to the uncertainty principle).
Explain that a nucleus is made up of protons and neutrons held together by the strong nuclear force.
Explain that an atomic model is an aid to understand the structure of an atom.
State the relative charge and relative masses of the subatomic particles (an electron, proton and neutron).
Interpret the relationship between a subatomic particle, its mass and charge.
Illustrate the path that positively and negatively charged particles would take under the influence of a uniform electric field.
Define proton number / atomic number as the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom.
Explain that the proton number is unique to each element and is used to arrange elements in the periodic table.
State that radioactivity can change the proton number and alter an atom's identity.
Define nucleon number / atomic mass as the sum of the number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom.
Define isotopes as different atoms of the same element that have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
State that isotopes can affect molecular mass but not the chemical properties of an atom.
Determine the number of protons and neutrons of different isotopes.
Define relative atomic mass as the average mass of isotopes of an element compared to 1/12th of the mass of an atom of carbon-12.
State that isotopes can exhibit radioactivity.
Discuss the importance of isotopes using carbon dating and medical imaging as examples.
Describe the formation of positive (cation) and negative (anion) ions from atoms.
Interpret and use the symbols for atoms and ions.
Calculate the relative atomic mass of an element from relative masses and abundance of isotopes.
Calculate the relative mass of an isotope given the relative atomic mass and abundance of all stable isotopes.

sections.heading: Atoms and the Discharge Tube
sections.body: Atoms were first named by Democritus for a particle that cannot be divided, and John Dalton's experiments gave evidence that atoms exist. Discharge tube experiments later showed that the atom is made of still smaller particles. A discharge tube is a hard glass tube with two metal electrodes and a vacuum pump, and electricity is passed through a gas at very low pressure. Rays from the cathode are cathode rays, and rays produced at the anode with a perforated cathode are canal rays.

sections.heading: Electrons, Protons and Neutrons
sections.body: J. J. Thomson showed that cathode rays are streams of negatively charged particles called electrons, which bend towards the positive plate in an electric field. Goldstein observed canal rays, which are positively charged, and the proton is the positive particle of the nucleus. The neutron has no charge and its mass is almost the same as that of a proton. A neutron is not deflected in an electric field, and ordinary hydrogen is the only atom that has no neutron.

sections.heading: The Nucleus and Fundamental Particles
sections.body: Rutherford hit a stream of special particles at a very thin gold foil and found that an atom has a tiny central nucleus with a large extranuclear region around it. The nucleus holds the protons and neutrons together by the strong nuclear force, while the electrons are found outside it. An atom is electrically neutral, so it contains equal numbers of electrons and protons. The electron is the lightest particle, and the proton is about 1836 times heavier than an electron.

sections.heading: Bohr's Atomic Model
sections.body: In Bohr's model the electron revolves around the nucleus in fixed circular paths called orbits or shells, and each shell has a fixed energy. The shells are energy levels labelled K, L, M and N, or n = 1, 2, 3 and 4. An electron in a shell far from the nucleus has more energy than one near it, and the nearest orbit is the ground state. The shell with number n contains n sub-shells, named s, p, d and f.

sections.heading: Modern Approach and Electron Arrangement
sections.body: The modern approach treats the electron as a quantum particle that behaves like a charged cloud. Only the probability of finding it can be given, and by the uncertainty principle its exact path cannot be mapped. The maximum number of electrons in a shell is 2n², so K holds 2, L holds 8, M holds 18 and N holds 32. The sub-shells hold at most 2 (s), 6 (p), 10 (d) and 14 (f) electrons. For the first 18 elements the arrangement is 2, then 8, then the rest in the M shell.

sections.heading: Atomic Number and Mass Number
sections.body: The atomic number Z is the number of protons in the nucleus, and it is unique to each element; elements are arranged in the periodic table by it. The mass number A is the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus. The number of neutrons is N = A − Z. An atom is written with A at the upper left and Z at the lower left of its symbol, for example ²³₁₁Na, and an ion has its charge at the upper right.

sections.heading: Isotopes
sections.body: Isotopes are atoms of the same element that have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. Hydrogen has three isotopes: protium ¹₁H with no neutron, deuterium ²₁H with one neutron and tritium ³₁H with two neutrons. Carbon has the isotopes ¹²₆C, ¹³₆C and ¹⁴₆C. Isotopes differ in mass and physical properties, but they have the same chemical properties.

sections.heading: Radioactive Isotopes and Their Uses
sections.body: Isotopes may be stable or radioactive. Radioactive isotopes have unstable nuclei and throw out radiation, and radioactivity can change the proton number and so change the identity of the atom. Carbon-14 is used in radiocarbon dating to find the age of wood or bone. Radioactive isotopes are used in medicine for imaging organs and treating diseases such as cancer, and in industry for testing metals and concrete.

sections.heading: Ions
sections.body: An atom becomes an ion when it loses or gains electrons, while its number of protons stays the same. An atom that loses electrons has more protons than electrons and becomes a positive ion, a cation, such as Na⁺ or Mg²⁺. An atom that gains electrons becomes a negative ion, an anion, such as Cl⁻ or O²⁻. Ionization can be caused by radiation of enough energy that forces a tightly bound electron away.

sections.heading: Relative Atomic Mass
sections.body: The relative atomic mass of an element is the average mass of its isotopes compared with 1/12th of the mass of a carbon-12 atom, which is one atomic mass unit. It is calculated by multiplying each isotopic mass by its percentage abundance, adding the products and dividing by 100. For an element with two isotopes the same method can be reversed to find an unknown abundance or the mass of one isotope.

definitions.definition: The smallest particle of an element, made of a nucleus and electrons; the word was first used by Democritus for a particle that cannot be divided.
A hard glass tube with two metallic electrodes and a vacuum pump, used to pass electricity through a gas at reduced pressure.
Rays emitted from the cathode of a discharge tube; they are streams of negatively charged electrons.
Rays produced at the anode of a discharge tube with a perforated cathode; they are positively charged (also called anode rays).
A negatively charged fundamental particle found outside the nucleus.
A positively charged fundamental particle found in the nucleus.
A fundamental particle with no charge found in the nucleus; its mass is almost the same as a proton.
The tiny central part of an atom that contains protons and neutrons.
The force that holds protons and neutrons together in the nucleus.
A fixed path around the nucleus in which an electron has a fixed energy; also called an energy level.
The state of an atom when its electron is in the orbit closest to the nucleus, with minimum energy.
A division of a shell: s, p, d or f; the number of sub-shells in a shell equals n.
The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom.
The sum of the number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom; also called nucleon number.
Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
The emission of excess energy in the form of radiation by unstable nuclei.
The change of a radioactive element into another element by emitting radiation.
A method of finding the age of an organic object by measuring the proportion of carbon-14 in it.
A positively charged ion formed when an atom loses one or more electrons.
A negatively charged ion formed when an atom gains one or more electrons.
The mass of an atom of an element relative to 1/12th of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
One-twelfth the mass of an atom of carbon-12; 1 amu = 1.67377 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.
The naturally occurring percentage of an isotope in an element.

examTips: Thomson found the electron (cathode rays), Goldstein found canal rays, Rutherford found the nucleus and Bohr proposed the shell model.
Remember the charges: electron −1, proton +1, neutron 0. The proton is about 1836 times heavier than the electron.
Atomic number Z = number of protons = number of electrons in a neutral atom. Mass number A = protons + neutrons.
Neutrons N = A − Z. Always subtract the lower left number from the upper left number.
Shell capacity is 2n²: K = 2, L = 8, M = 18, N = 32. Sub-shells hold 2, 6, 10 and 14 electrons (s, p, d, f).
For the first 18 elements fill K (2), then L (8), then M. For example chlorine (Z = 17) is 2, 8, 7.
Isotopes: same Z, different A, same chemical properties. Atoms with the same A but different Z are not isotopes.
Cation = loses electrons = positive. Anion = gains electrons = negative. Protons never change when an ion forms.
Relative atomic mass = (m₁ × %₁ + m₂ × %₂) / 100, and the abundances of all isotopes add up to 100%.
Link uses to isotopes: carbon-14 for dating, technetium-99m for medical imaging, radioactive isotopes for treating cancer.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Who showed that cathode rays are streams of negatively charged electrons?
practiceQuestions.explanation: J. J. Thomson studied cathode rays and showed they are negatively charged particles called electrons.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Canal rays were observed by Goldstein when the cathode of the discharge tube was
practiceQuestions.explanation: Goldstein used a perforated cathode, and the canal rays passed through its holes.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which scientist discovered the nucleus of the atom in his gold foil experiment?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Rutherford hit special particles at a thin gold foil and concluded that the atom has a tiny central nucleus.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which particle in the nucleus carries a positive charge?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The proton is the positively charged particle in the nucleus; the neutron has no charge.

practiceQuestions.prompt: How many neutrons are present in an atom of ²³₁₁Na?
What is the maximum number of electrons that the M shell (n = 3) can hold?
Isotopes of an element have the same number of
practiceQuestions.explanation: Isotopes have the same number of protons (same atomic number) but different numbers of neutrons.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Chlorine has two isotopes: mass 35 (75%) and mass 37 (25%). What is its relative atomic mass?

practiceQuestions.explanation: The neutron is a neutral particle, so it is not deflected in an electric field.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Isotopes of an element have different chemical properties.
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. Isotopes have the same chemical properties but differ in their physical properties.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The mass number of an atom is the sum of its protons and neutrons.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The mass number A is the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus.

practiceQuestions.prompt: In the modern approach the exact path of an electron can be mapped.
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. Electrons are quantum particles, so only the probability of finding them can be stated.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom is called its ____ number.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The number of protons in the nucleus is the atomic number (proton number).

practiceQuestions.prompt: Atoms of the same element with different mass numbers are called ____.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Isotopes have the same atomic number but different mass numbers.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An atom that loses an electron becomes a positively charged ion called a ____.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Losing electrons leaves more protons than electrons, giving a positive ion called a cation.

sequencingActivity.explanation: Take a thin gold foil, hit it with a stream of special particles, observe their behaviour, and conclude that the atom has a tiny nucleus surrounded by a large extranuclear region.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: A species has 19 protons, 20 neutrons and 18 electrons. Which statement is correct?

options: It is an anion with charge −1 and mass number 39
It is a cation with charge +1 and mass number 39
It is a neutral atom with mass number 39
It is a cation with charge +2 and mass number 38

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: Charge = 19 − 18 = +1, so it is a cation, and the mass number is 19 + 20 = 39.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: Which pair consists of isotopes of the same element?
bossBattleQuestions.explanation: Both carbon atoms have 6 protons but different neutrons. The other pairs are different elements or an atom and its ion.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: An element has two isotopes: mass 10 (20%) and mass 11 (80%). What is its relative atomic mass?
Why do isotopes of an element have the same chemical properties?

options: They have the same mass number
They have the same number of neutrons
They have the same number of electrons and protons; only the neutrons differ
They have different numbers of electrons

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: Chemical properties depend on the electrons, which are equal in isotopes; only the neutron number and mass differ.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: What is the arrangement of electrons (K, L, M) in the Mg²⁺ ion (Z = 12)?
bossBattleQuestions.explanation: Mg²⁺ has 12 − 2 = 10 electrons, so it is 2, 8.
